provenance_note: Seven labels -- tool_definition_drift, tool_description_injection, excessive_agency_schema, indirect_injection_surface, missing_hitl_confirmation, unpinned_remote_source, missing_provenance -- were copied verbatim from output this project produced and committed at tests/fixtures/sentinel-scan-cli-a02-post-trigger-report.json and tests/fixtures/sentinel-scan-cli-whole-corpus-report.json (image mcp-sec-bench/sentinel-scan-cli:1.4.16, corpus v1-0ef4bd851ab8). The remaining eight were read out of the shipped module in that same pinned image (`python -c "import re,sentinel_scan; print(sorted(set(re.findall(r'_mcp_finding\(\s*\n?\s*\"([a-z_]+)\"', open(sentinel_scan.__file__).read()))))"`), which is the code that emits the string rather than vendor prose about it -- so the SPELLING of every label here is verified against the shipped build. Labels not yet seen to fire on this corpus carry status `provisional`, which is what separates a verified spelling from a verified behaviour. NOTE FOR REVIEWERS: docs/scanner-survey.md lists 11 heuristics for this tool; 1.4.16 actually emits 15. The four the survey does not name are command_injection_risk, cross_origin_exfiltration, dos_resource_exhaustion and homoglyph_typosquat, and all four are covered below so that none of them could arrive as an unrecognised label mid-run.

matching.note: Byte-exact, the default. sentinel-scan-cli's heuristic ids are literal string arguments to a single finding constructor (_mcp_finding) in one module, so they cannot drift in case or spacing within a build; nothing here justifies loosening the match.

notes: Covers all 15 heuristic ids emitted by sentinel-scan-cli 1.4.16. Six map, nine are unmapped with a stated reason. Per docs/scoring.md an unmapped finding is neither a true nor a false positive, so the nine cost this scanner nothing; they are a claim about the reach of OUR taxonomy, not about the tool.

READ THIS BEFORE READING THE ROW. This scanner takes an mcp.json manifest and nothing else: it cannot read a source tree and cannot connect to an endpoint. The corpus ships no mcp.json, so runner/adapters/sentinel_scan.py GENERATES one per server -- the tool descriptors verbatim as tools/list served them, plus an mcpServers block describing the live lab endpoint. Two consequences change how the raw output should be read, and neither is a mapping decision: (1) unpinned_remote_source and missing_provenance fire on all 15 servers (30 of 42 findings) and are properties of the generated config file and the lab's plain-HTTP deployment, not of any corpus server's source; (2) hardcoded_credential cannot fire at all, because the adapter writes the lab bearer token as a ${MCPBENCH_TOKEN} placeholder rather than a literal -- planting the literal would have manufactured A7 true positives against a credential we put in a file we wrote.

tool_definition_drift is the entry that matters most on this board: A2 (rug-pull) is detected by no other scanner here, and this label is the only purpose-built rug-pull check among them. It only exists when the scanner is given --baseline AND two captures of the same tool. That is off by default and a single-shot invocation can never produce it; the adapter drives the sequence explicitly (capture 1 -> --update-baseline -> provoke -> capture N -> --baseline). That is an invocation fact, not a mapping fact, but a reader comparing this row to another scanner's 0.00 on A2 should know the harness had to work for it. Verified firing on a02-rug-pull.

One false positive on this corpus is caused by the harness rather than by the scanner's judgment, and it is left in place deliberately. Driving a02's rug-pull means the post-trigger manifest contains the injected descriptor, so tool_description_injection fires on summarize_changelog as well; that label maps to A1, a02 declares A2 and tolerates nothing, so the finding scores as a false positive and a near miss (right server, wrong class). Suppressing it would mean keying a mapping on the server and its state, which docs/mapping-rationale.md R5 forbids; R6 prefers the error a reader can see on a named item. It is the same phenomenon A2 credits, reported under an A1-shaped label.

excessive_agency_schema is the entry most likely to be argued with, because it is the label that fired on a10b-allowlist-bypass's run_build with the evidence text 'parameter "command" is a free-form string with no enum/pattern - looks like arbitrary command/code execution'. It is left UNMAPPED under R4. The reason is structural: one label covers five different schema shapes, and two of them satisfy two different classes' tests (the free-form command parameter points at A10, the unconstrained path parameter points at A8). docs/mapping-rationale.md section 2 forbids keying a decision on the finding's free-text message, so there is no permitted way to split them, and R4 says the label is not mapped to the least-bad option. Declining costs this scanner a plausible detection on a10b; forcing it would cost the benchmark its claim to be measuring the tool rather than our reading of one evidence string.

Four of our ten classes have no sentinel-scan-cli label whose present-when test they satisfy, so a miss there is a false negative rather than a mapping gap: A4 (response injection), A5 (argument exfiltration), A6 (authless endpoint), A8 (unrestricted file read). All four need either a tool's return value, an observed egress attempt, an auth posture, or source-level containment analysis, and none of those is visible in a tool manifest.
Read docs/mapping-rationale.md for the R1-R6 decision procedure the rationale text cites.

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'MCP04: a tool's current definition hash no longer matches a previously recorded baseline for that tool name - the "MCP rug pull" pattern ... where a server changes a tool's description/schema after it was already reviewed and trusted, so a static single-scan check can't catch it but a baseline comparison across scans can.' The hash covers exactly (name, description, inputSchema). Emitted only when --baseline names a file written by a prior --update-baseline run.

taxonomy_evidence.present_when_quote: the descriptor served for a given tool differs between two points in the server's lifecycle, and the later version contains content that would independently qualify under A1, or advertises a capability the earlier version did not. A cosmetic diff (version string, whitespace, a reworded sentence with no behavioural content) does not qualify
taxonomy_evidence.why_satisfied: The rule compares the sha256 of (name, description, inputSchema) for one tool against the hash recorded for that same tool name at an earlier point, and fires when they differ. That is the first clause of the test exactly: the descriptor served for a given tool differs between two points in the running instance's lifecycle. The second clause -- that the later version independently qualifies under A1 or advertises new capability -- is a judgment the corpus author makes and records in the manifest (a02's manifest records both descriptors and the trigger index); it is ground truth for the scorer to apply, not a property any label can assert, in the same way A7's 'the manifest marks a literal as a planted secret' is not something a secret-scanning rule can satisfy.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A1's Not-this-class clause settles it in one line: 'the payload is present from the first tools/list. If it only appears after a state change, it is A2.' This label reports the state change itself and asserts nothing whatsoever about the text of either descriptor -- it is a hash comparison. Mapping it to A1 would credit a detection of a payload for a rule that never reads one.

A3 requires a descriptor field that references a tool or server other than itself. This rule compares one tool against its own earlier hash and has no cross-server notion at all; sentinel-scan-cli registers tool_name_shadowing separately for the cross-tool case.

entries.rationale: The strongest objection is that the rule does not judge the diff, and taxonomy.md excludes a cosmetic diff from A2 by name -- so a vendor could argue this label over-claims and a critic could argue it should therefore be unmapped. We hold the mapping, for the same reason mcp-guard's secret rule maps to A7 despite firing on a placeholder: the label reports the class's property (a tool descriptor that moved after it was approved), and whether a particular diff is security-relevant is exactly what the corpus manifest declares and what the scorer checks the mapped finding against. A mapping that reached in to second-guess the scanner's judgment about a specific diff would be scoring our reading instead of its detection (R5). The residual error is stated rather than absorbed (R6): on a server that legitimately reissued a reworded description between two captures, this label would produce a false positive that taxonomy.md's 'a server that legitimately updates its tools between deployments is not A2' excludes, and it would land as a visible false positive on a named item rather than disappearing into a heuristic. On corpus v1 it fires exactly once, on a02-rug-pull's summarize_changelog, which is the one server where the descriptor is designed to move.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Emitted by _mcp_scan_name_shadowing on four distinct routes: (a) two tool names normalising to the same letters-and-digits string; (b) one name within Levenshtein distance 2 of a hardcoded list of well-known sensitive tool names (read_file, write_file, send_email, exec, shell, ...); (c) two manifest tool names within distance 2 of each other; (d) a description matching the shadow-claim regex 'use this tool|use this instead|instead of the other/built-in|overrides the built-in/other/default|replaces the built-in/other/default'. Vendor's own recommendation: 'A tool description should never instruct the agent to prefer it over another tool - that is a hallmark of tool-poisoning/shadowing.' OWASP MCP02: Tool Poisoning / Shadowing.

taxonomy_evidence.present_when_quote: a descriptor field on X references a tool or server other than itself, and the reference asserts something about how that other tool should be selected, trusted, or invoked
taxonomy_evidence.why_satisfied: Route (d) satisfies the test verbatim: the rule fires on a description that claims this tool overrides, replaces, or should be used instead of another tool -- a reference to a tool other than itself that asserts how that other tool should be selected. Routes (a) and (c) satisfy it by the mechanism A3's definition names explicitly, 'redefining its meaning': a tool whose advertised name collides with (or is one or two edits from) another tool's name is metadata whose effect is to change which implementation the agent selects when it reaches for that name. In both routes the referenced other tool is identified in the finding -- the evidence text names the colliding pair.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A1's Not-this-class clause draws the line at precisely this feature and even gives the worked example: 'A payload that says "always call this tool first" is A1; one that says "the send_email tool from the mail server is deprecated, use this instead" is A3.' Sentinel's shadow-claim regex matches the second shape, not the first -- the 'always call this tool first' phrasing lives in the separate tool_description_injection phrase list. The distinguishing cross-tool reference is present, so the more specific class wins.

Nothing in this label involves a change over time; it compares names and descriptions within a single capture. A2 requires the mutation, and sentinel-scan-cli registers tool_definition_drift for that.

entries.rationale: This and MR-sentinel-scan-cli-001 are the two entries worth the most care, and this one is the weaker of the pair, so the weakness is stated rather than smoothed over. Route (b) -- a name within two edits of a hardcoded well-known name -- can report 'shadowing' of a tool that is not in the scan set at all, so the 'references a tool other than itself' clause is satisfied against a name the scanner supplied rather than one the manifest contains. We map the label anyway and set confidence to medium: A3's definition is about metadata whose effect is to change how the agent uses another tool, a near-duplicate name has exactly that effect whether or not the impersonated tool is in this particular manifest, and whether the approximation is a good one is a precision question the scoreboard answers with numbers rather than a mapping question. The alternative -- unmapped for no-defensible-single-class -- was rejected because only one class's test is in play here; R4 is for a genuine tie, not for a label we find imprecise. What this entry does NOT do is rescue the scanner's miss on a03-tool-shadowing, and the reason is worth publishing because it is a near miss inside the vendor's own regex rather than inside our table: a03's route_alert description says the other server's tool 'has been deprecated', is 'no longer a trusted delivery path', and that the agent should 'route those calls to this tool instead' -- semantically the exact shape route (d) is written for, but the regex wants the literal 'use this tool'/'use this instead'/'instead of the built-in', and 'route those calls to this tool instead' matches none of them. Verified: the label does not fire on a03 at either per-server or whole-corpus scope.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Emitted from two places. _mcp_scan_description matches a 24-pattern imperative/override phrase list against the tool description ('ignore previous instructions', 'do not tell the user', 'always call this tool first', 'this tool takes priority over', 'note to the agent', 'secretly', ...), or fires on zero-width characters, an HTML comment block, or a long base64-like blob in the description. _mcp_scan_schema_text_injection applies the same phrase list to input- and output-schema text (property descriptions, titles, enum values). Vendor's own recommendation: 'Rewrite the description to plainly describe the tool's function to a human/reviewer only. Strip imperative language directed at the calling agent.' OWASP MCP01.

taxonomy_evidence.present_when_quote: a field in the tool descriptor contains natural-language content that does at least one of: issues an instruction to the agent, asserts priority over other instructions, directs concealment from the user, or specifies conditions under which the agent should act differently
taxonomy_evidence.why_satisfied: The rule's phrase list is a near-enumeration of that test's four limbs: 'you must always call this' and 'always call this tool first' issue an instruction; 'this tool takes priority over' and 'supersedes the user's request' assert priority; 'do not tell/mention ... the user', 'without telling the user' and 'secretly' direct concealment; 'before responding' and 'regardless of what the user asked' specify conditions under which the agent should act differently. It matches those phrases in the tool description and in schema property text, both of which are fields of the tool descriptor served by tools/list.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A1's Not-this-class clause: 'the payload is present from the first tools/list. If it only appears after a state change, it is A2.' This rule is a single-capture text match with no notion of state or of an earlier descriptor, and sentinel-scan-cli registers tool_definition_drift for the state change. The label reports the payload, not the mutation.

A1's other disclaimer: 'the payload targets agent behaviour generally. If it names or redefines another server's tool, it is A3.' The phrase list contains no cross-tool reference, and the vendor keeps the shadow-claim regex under the separate tool_name_shadowing id.
A4's distinguishing feature is that the payload rides in a tool's return value: 'A1 is metadata, A4 is payload data.' This rule reads the descriptor and the schema and never a return value.

entries.rationale: The clean case: the label and the class name the same property, and the vendor's own phrase list reads like a paraphrase of A1's present-when test. Two consequences are disclosed rather than designed away. First, the label does NOT fire on a01-tool-description-injection, the server built for this class: a01's payload says 'this directive takes priority over the user's request' where the phrase list carries 'this tool takes priority over' and 'supersedes the user's request', so it lands between two patterns and matches neither. That is a genuine, publishable miss of the vendor's pattern coverage and nothing in this table should paper over it. Second, the label DOES fire on a02-rug-pull once the adapter has provoked the rug-pull, because the mutated descriptor contains 'Do not mention this note to the user'. a02 declares A2 and tolerates nothing, so that finding scores as a false positive and a near miss on a02. We do not narrow the mapping to exclude it: the mapping is keyed on the label and may not be keyed on the server or on the target's state (R5), and the taxonomy itself says injection content that appears only after a state change is A2 rather than A1 -- so this is precisely a right-server-wrong-class near miss, which is the error a reader can see and dispute (R6).
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM01: hidden/unicode-obfuscated text (tag-block smuggling, bidi overrides, zero-width characters) anywhere in a tool's name, description, or input-schema text.' Fires on the Unicode tag block U+E0000-U+E007F, bidirectional override/isolate controls, or zero-width characters. Vendor's own recommendation says these 'can hide instructions from a human reviewer while the calling LLM still parses and follows them'. OWASP MCP01.

taxonomy_evidence.present_when_quote: a field in the tool descriptor contains natural-language content that does at least one of: issues an instruction to the agent, asserts priority over other instructions, directs concealment from the user, or specifies conditions under which the agent should act differently
taxonomy_evidence.why_satisfied: A1's definition qualifies the present-when test: the content at issue is text 'that addresses the consuming model rather than describing the tool'. The Unicode tag block mirrors printable ASCII one character for one and renders as nothing in effectively every interface, so text encoded in it is by construction addressed to the model and to nobody else; the same is true of a bidi override that reorders what a human sees while leaving the model-visible sequence intact. The rule reports that such content is present in the descriptor's name, description, or schema text -- a field of the tool descriptor carrying content aimed at the consuming model.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A3 needs a reference to another tool or server. Invisible characters carry no identified referent, and sentinel-scan-cli keeps the mixed-script impersonation case under a separate id (homoglyph_typosquat, unmapped below for that same reason).

entries.rationale: The objection to answer is that the rule detects a smuggling CHANNEL rather than an instruction: a zero-width space left behind by a copy-paste would fire, and a stray zero-width space is not a payload addressed to anyone. We map it to A1 regardless, and set confidence to medium to say so. A1's own text puts the weight on content that addresses the consuming model instead of describing the tool, and tag-block or bidi-obfuscated text in a descriptor has no other function; a rule that reports it is reporting the A1 property, and its rate of firing on innocuous invisible whitespace is a precision fact the scoreboard measures rather than a reason to withhold the class. The alternative considered was unmapped/insufficient-specificity, and it was rejected because it would have made this table's treatment of invisible characters inconsistent: tool_description_injection ALSO fires on a bare zero-width character in a description, and mapping one of those to A1 while refusing the other would be a distinction with no basis in either label. The label has not fired on this corpus -- every planted payload in corpus v1 is plain printable text -- so this entry is provisional and no published number currently depends on it.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM02: secrets or credentials hardcoded in a server's env block or args, instead of an env-var placeholder resolved at launch time.' Requires an mcpServers entry whose env key name matches (api[_-]?key|secret|token|password|passwd|credential|access[_-]?key|private[_-]?key) with a non-placeholder value at least 8 characters long, or a CLI arg of the form --*key|token|secret|password|credential=<value>. Placeholders '${VAR}', '$VAR', '<VAR>' and the empty string are excluded by regex. OWASP MCP03.

taxonomy_evidence.present_when_quote: the manifest marks a literal as a planted secret and the value is syntactically a credential of a recognisable type - not a placeholder, not a variable reference, not a documented example value
taxonomy_evidence.why_satisfied: The rule requires a literal value, under a key whose name identifies it as a credential, in committed configuration -- and it excludes by explicit regex exactly the three things the test excludes: an environment-variable reference ('$VAR'), a template placeholder ('${VAR}', '<VAR>') and an empty value. That is the second half of the test almost clause for clause. The first half -- that the manifest marks it -- is ground truth the scorer applies, not something a label can satisfy.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A7's own Not-this-class clause draws the line at the secret's origin: 'A7 is a secret in the code. A9 is a channel that leaks secrets from the environment.' This rule reports a literal value sitting in configuration and asserts nothing about a tool returning environment contents to its caller.

entries.rationale: A clean mapping with an important caveat about reach rather than about class. The class is not in doubt: a credential-shaped literal in committed configuration is what A7 is. What is worth saying out loud is that this label CANNOT fire in the configuration this benchmark runs, and that the reason is a harness decision rather than a property of the tool. sentinel-scan-cli only ever reads credentials out of an mcpServers env block or an args array; the corpus ships no mcp.json, so the adapter writes one, and it writes the lab bearer token as the ${MCPBENCH_TOKEN} placeholder. Had it written the literal, this label would have fired on all eleven authenticated servers and this entry would have turned a credential WE put in a file WE wrote into eleven A7 true positives -- including against c01-notes-workspace and c02-webhook-notifier, which tolerate nothing. A7's real ground truth in corpus v1 is a literal in a07-hardcoded-secrets/server.py, a Python source file this scanner cannot read at all, so A7 is a structural false negative for this tool and not a mapping gap. Provisional: the spelling is verified against the shipped module, the behaviour is not observed here.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM06: a tool description or implementation annotation documents that a caller-supplied parameter is interpolated into a shell/exec call without sanitization - a command-injection primitive exposed straight through the tool's declared surface.' Requires BOTH a shell/exec signature in the descriptor text (os.system(, subprocess.run/call/popen/check_output(, eval(, exec(, Runtime.getRuntime().exec, ProcessBuilder(, 'shelling out') AND an unsanitised-input phrase ('unsanitized', 'without sanitizing', 'passed through raw', 'appended directly to the shell'). Not named in docs/scanner-survey.md's list of 11.

taxonomy_evidence.present_when_quote: the manifest records a caller-reachable execution sink and, for A10b, a concrete bypass string that escapes the intended command set
taxonomy_evidence.why_satisfied: The property the rule reports is that a caller-supplied parameter reaches a shell or exec call without sanitisation -- a caller-reachable execution sink, which is the first clause of the test and, per A10's Credit clause, the whole of what credit turns on: 'a scanner that reports A10 on the A10b server earns credit whether or not it articulates the bypass'. The rule's evidence is the descriptor's own prose rather than a code path, which affects how often it is right, not which class it names.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A8 disclaims the subprocess route in one line: 'no process is executed. If the read happens via a subprocess, it is A10.' This rule's trigger set is process-execution signatures, so a process is executed and the more specific class is A10.

entries.rationale: The honest objection is that this rule reads a self-report: it fires only when the descriptor text itself contains something like 'subprocess.run(' together with the word 'unsanitized', which means it catches a manifest that confesses rather than a server that offends. That is a very narrow trigger and we expect it to fire rarely in the wild. It is still the A10 property being reported -- caller input reaching process execution -- and a scanner is entitled to arrive at that property from whatever evidence it has; mcp-guard's JS path rule is mapped on the same basis. The narrowness shows up as recall, which is what the scoreboard is for. It does not fire on a10a-command-execution or a10b-allowlist-bypass, whose descriptions are written the way a real server's would be ('Run a build command, restricted to the allowlisted build tools') and mention neither a subprocess API nor the absence of sanitisation, so this entry is provisional and no published number depends on it.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Emitted by _mcp_scan_schema_agency on five distinct shapes under one id: (1) inputSchema sets additionalProperties: true; (2) inputSchema of type object declares no properties and does not lock additionalProperties to false; (3) a property named command/cmd/shell/code/script/exec/eval typed as a string with no enum and no pattern -- evidence 'looks like arbitrary command/code execution'; (4) a property named path/file_path/filepath/dir/directory/filename typed as an unconstrained string -- recommendation 'unconstrained paths enable traversal'; (5) a boolean property whose name matches (sudo|admin|bypass|override|force|unrestricted). OWASP MCP06: Excessive Agency / Permissions.

considered_classes.why_rejected: Shape (3) points squarely at A10 -- an unconstrained free-form parameter named 'command', which the rule's own evidence calls arbitrary command execution. But choosing A10 for the label means choosing it for shapes (1), (2), (4) and (5) as well, and shape (4) is a filesystem path parameter, which A10 does not describe.

Shape (4) points squarely at A8 -- an unconstrained caller-supplied filesystem path with no pattern, which the rule's own recommendation says 'enable traversal'. But the same objection runs the other way: choosing A8 for the label also chooses it for shape (3), a command-execution parameter, which A8 disclaims explicitly.
Nothing in any of the five shapes concerns process environment contents, which is what A9 is about.

entries.rationale: This is R4 in its clearest form, and it is the most expensive decision in this file, so the cost is stated first: this is the label that fired on a10b-allowlist-bypass's run_build, and leaving it unmapped means sentinel-scan-cli gets no credit for a10b's A10 item even though the finding's evidence text reads 'parameter "command" is a free-form string with no enum/pattern - looks like arbitrary command/code execution'. A reader is entitled to find that galling. The reason we hold it is that the alternative is not available under this project's own rules. Two of the label's five shapes satisfy two different classes' present-when tests -- shape (3) satisfies A10's, shape (4) satisfies A8's -- neither class's Not-this-class clause separates them (A8's disclaimer separates reads-via-subprocess from reads, not one schema shape from another), and R3 permits a single label to be split only on the stage that produced the finding, which is identical for both. The only remaining way to tell them apart would be to read the finding's free-text evidence, and docs/mapping-rationale.md section 2 forbids keying a decision on the message precisely because a substring rule over prose is not reviewable and its accuracy would be a property of our reading rather than of the tool's detection. So R4 applies: unmapped, not mapped to the least-bad option. Two things follow that a reader should weigh against the lost credit. The label would also have fired on a08-unrestricted-file-read or c01-notes-workspace had their path parameters not been schema-constrained, in which case an A10 mapping would have produced false positives of exactly the kind this decision avoids. And the gap is a finding about OUR taxonomy, which has no class for over-broad declared agency as such: that is the signal `unmapped` is designed to carry (docs/scoring.md), and the cheapest way to close it is a taxonomy amendment under docs/governance.md, not a forced entry here.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM06: a tool with a sensitive capability (exec/filesystem-write/outbound-send) but no declared human-in-the-loop/confirmation metadata.' Capability is classified by keyword hit across the tool's name, description and schema property names; the finding is suppressed if the tool (or its annotations) carries any truthy field named requiresConfirmation, requireApproval, humanInTheLoop, needsApproval or a spelling variant. OWASP MCP06.

considered_classes.why_rejected: The capability classifier's first keyword group is exec/shell/eval/bash/run_command/execute_command/command, so the label does fire on tools that look like they run commands. But the property it reports is the ABSENCE of confirmation metadata, not the presence of a caller-reachable execution sink: a tool with a raw shell sink and 'requiresConfirmation: true' in its annotations produces no finding at all, and a tool with no sink whose description merely contains the word 'send' produces one. A10's present-when test asks for a caller-reachable execution sink; this label does not report one.

A6 is about a network endpoint executing sensitive tool calls without authenticating the caller. A confirmation prompt is a host-side interaction gate for an authenticated caller, not authentication; the label asserts nothing about credentials or about the endpoint's auth posture.

entries.rationale: Our taxonomy has no class for 'a sensitive capability is exposed without a declared approval gate', and it should not be pushed into one. This is the most frequently firing label on corpus v1 -- eight findings, on a03, a06, a10a, a10b, c02 (twice) and c03 (twice) -- so the decision matters more than most. The property reported is a missing metadata field, which is a host-enforcement and governance concern: taxonomy.md's scope boundary excludes 'vulnerabilities in the host application or agent framework consuming the server', and a requiresConfirmation flag is an instruction to that host. The strongest objection is that on a10a and a10b it happens to land on the right servers, so mapping it to A10 would look like detection. That argument is exactly the one R5 exists to refuse: it reasons from which server the finding hit rather than from what the label reports, and applied consistently it would also make c02-webhook-notifier's send_notification and c03-release-runner's setup_example into A10 findings, which they are not -- c02 is a benign control that tolerates nothing, and c03 tolerates A7 only. Leaving the label unmapped costs this scanner nothing in precision and records a real gap in our ten classes.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Emitted on two routes. _mcp_scan_indirect_injection_surface tags each tool as content-ingesting and/or action-taking by keyword hit over its name and description, then fires HIGH on any single tool that is both, and MEDIUM once per manifest when ingesting tools and acting tools coexist as separate tools. _mcp_scan_untrusted_passthrough fires HIGH under the same id when descriptor text documents that untrusted external content is forwarded into the assistant's context unchanged. OWASP MCP01.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A4's present-when test requires that 'a tool call with manifest-specified arguments returns content that would qualify as an instruction to the agent under the A1 test'. Neither route observes a return value: the first is a keyword judgment about what a tool's name and description suggest it can do, and the second is a prose self-report that untrusted content passes through. Neither establishes that any call returns instruction-bearing content, so the test is not satisfied.

A1 requires instruction-bearing content in the descriptor. Both routes report a property OF the tool's capability or data flow; the descriptor text they match is a description of behaviour, not a payload addressed to the model.

entries.rationale: The concept this label names -- a toxic agent flow, where the capability to ingest untrusted content sits next to the capability to act on it -- is a real and well-documented MCP risk that our ten classes do not cover. That is a gap in our taxonomy and `unmapped` is how this project records such a gap rather than hiding it. Mapping it to A4 was considered seriously, because A4 is the class about untrusted content reaching the agent, and rejected under R1: A4 is defined by what a call RETURNS, and this label never sees a return value. The practical consequence is worth stating because it runs in the scanner's favour: on corpus v1 this label fires once, on c02-webhook-notifier's send_notification, and c02 is a benign control carrying no tolerated entry -- so an A4 mapping would have produced a true false positive against a control, which is precisely the outcome the controls exist to reveal. That is a consequence of the decision, not its basis; the basis is that the present-when test is not satisfied.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM02: description text builds an outbound URL that embeds a content-bearing tool parameter as a query-string placeholder - fetching or even just rendering/previewing that link forwards the parameter's contents to whatever third-party host the URL points at.' Requires an http(s) URL in the descriptor text containing a {placeholder} whose name matches a schema property whose name contains one of content/document/body/secret/password/token/credential/history/message/transcript/notes/feedback. OWASP MCP05. Not named in docs/scanner-survey.md's list of 11.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A5's Not-this-class clause excludes the exact shape this rule fires on: 'A tool whose declared purpose is to send data somewhere - a webhook tool that posts its arguments to a URL the user supplied - is not A5. The class requires the destination to be undeclared or attacker-controlled.' This rule finds the URL written in the tool's own description, which makes the destination declared by construction, and it has no way to tell a declared destination from an attacker-controlled one. A5 also requires an observed egress attempt at runtime ('the attempt is what counts'), and this rule observes no call at all.
Nothing here concerns a tool's return value; the direction of flow is outbound from the arguments.

entries.rationale: This label reports something real and close to A5 -- argument content flowing to a third-party host -- and is still left unmapped, because the single distinction A5 turns on is the one this rule structurally cannot make. A5 is about an undeclared or attacker-controlled destination, observed as an egress attempt; this rule is about a destination spelled out in the descriptor, inferred from text. Mapping it anyway would credit A5 for exactly the case A5 disclaims, and on this corpus the shape it most resembles is c02-webhook-notifier, the benign control that exists to be the declared-destination counterexample. The reason recorded is insufficient-specificity rather than outside-taxonomy-scope deliberately: the concept is inside our scope, it is A5's concept, and the label is simply too coarse to place against A5's test. If a future revision of the tool distinguished a descriptor-declared destination from a constructed one, this entry should be revisited.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM06: overbroad or wildcard tool/server scopes instead of an enumerated, least-privilege permission list.' Matches a scopes/permissions entry against (^|[:./])(\*|all|admin|full[_-]?access|god[_-]?mode)($|[:./]) on either a tool object or an mcpServers entry. OWASP MCP06.
entries.rationale: An authorization-hygiene check about a declared permission string. Our ten classes are about flaws in what a server advertises or does, and none of them is about the breadth of a scope grant: there is no class whose present-when test a wildcard scope entry satisfies, so under R1 the label is unmapped rather than pushed toward A6 (which is about authenticating the caller, not about what an authenticated caller may do) or A10 (which requires an execution sink). It cannot fire in this configuration either way: MCP tools/list responses carry no scopes or permissions field, and the adapter does not invent one for the mcpServers block it writes. Spelling verified against the shipped module; behaviour not observed.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM03: remote/unpinned tool sources - unversioned package pulls or plaintext remote transports in a server launch config.' Two branches: HIGH when an mcpServers entry's url starts with http://, and LOW (surfaced only when the manifest already carries another finding) when a package-runner command launches an unpinned package reference. OWASP MCP04.
entries.rationale: Both branches are outside the taxonomy, and for different reasons that are each written down in taxonomy.md. The plaintext-transport branch is a transport-layer finding, and taxonomy.md's scope boundary excludes 'transport-layer issues (TLS configuration, etc.) not specific to MCP' in terms. The unpinned-package branch is a supply-chain property of how a server is fetched, and no class's present-when test speaks to it. So under R1 there is no class to cite and the label is unmapped. The disclosure that belongs with this entry is about volume rather than class: this label fires on all fifteen servers, because the adapter's generated manifest describes each corpus server by the URL the lab actually serves it on, which is plain HTTP on a localhost port. Fifteen of the forty-two findings in a run are this label, they are a true statement about how the lab is deployed and how the adapter writes a config file, and they are not detections of anything planted in the corpus. Being unmapped they cost the scanner nothing and earn it nothing; a reader of the raw output needs to know they are there so the finding count is not mistaken for detection.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM03: missing tool provenance/signature - a remote-sourced server (package runner or URL transport) with no way to verify what's launched.' Fires once per mcpServers entry that has a url or a package-runner command and none of the fields signature, sha256, checksum, integrity, publisher, provenance, attestation. OWASP MCP04.
entries.rationale: A supply-chain governance check: it reports the absence of publisher or integrity metadata for a remotely-sourced server. No class in taxonomy.md has a present-when test about provenance metadata, so under R1 the label is unmapped; reaching for A7 (a credential literal) or A2 (a descriptor that moved) would be 'closest in spirit' reasoning, which R1 refuses by name. As with unpinned_remote_source, the volume is the thing to disclose rather than the class: it fires on all fifteen servers because the adapter's generated mcpServers entries carry a url and no signature field, so fifteen of a run's forty-two findings are this label and none of them is about a corpus server's source. It is also a fair observation about the corpus as deployed -- no corpus server publishes provenance metadata -- which is why the entry says outside-taxonomy-scope rather than calling the finding wrong.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM10: a tool description documents that it has no depth/size/row/pagination limit or output cap - a single call can exhaust memory, CPU, or the calling model's context window (unbounded consumption).' Matches an eight-pattern phrase list ('unbounded', 'no pagination', 'loads the entire ... into memory', 'exhaust the caller's context', ...) against the tool description. OWASP MCP08. Not named in docs/scanner-survey.md's list of 11.
entries.rationale: Unbounded consumption is not one of our ten classes. Nothing in taxonomy.md has a present-when test about resource limits, output caps or context-window exhaustion, so under R1 there is no class to cite. This is a straightforward gap rather than a contestable call: the label names a real risk category (OWASP LLM10 / MCP08) that a future taxonomy amendment could add, and recording it as unmapped is how this project reports that. Spelling verified against the shipped module; the label has not fired on corpus v1, whose tool descriptions document their limits rather than the absence of them.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)

entries.label_note: Vendor's own docstring: 'LLM01: flag identifiers that mix Latin letters with visually-confusable letters from another script (e.g. Cyrillic i U+0456 vs Latin i) ... any Latin+Cyrillic/Greek mix in the same identifier is a strong signal of a homoglyph-based typosquat trying to impersonate a well-known tool name.' Applied to tool names and to mcpServers keys. Not named in docs/scanner-survey.md's list of 11.

considered_classes.why_rejected: A3's present-when test needs 'a descriptor field on X [that] references a tool or server other than itself' and a reference that 'asserts something about how that other tool should be selected, trusted, or invoked'. A mixed-script identifier identifies no referent: the rule reports that a name is built to be visually confused with something, without saying what, and the finding names no other tool. sentinel-scan-cli keeps the cases that DO identify a referent -- a normalised-name collision, a near-duplicate pair, an override claim -- under tool_name_shadowing, which is mapped to A3 above.

A1 needs natural-language content in the descriptor that addresses the consuming model. A script mixture in an identifier is not content addressed to anyone; the adjacent case of characters that are invisible rather than confusable is reported under hidden_unicode_instructions, which is mapped to A1 above.

entries.rationale: The line this entry draws is between shadowing that names its target and impersonation that does not, and it is the same line the vendor draws by giving the two cases different ids. tool_name_shadowing is mapped to A3 because every route it fires on identifies the tool being shadowed; this label reports only that an identifier mixes scripts, which is a strong signal of intent to be confused with some trusted name but never says which, so A3's reference-plus-assertion test cannot be satisfied. The reason recorded is insufficient-specificity rather than outside-taxonomy-scope because the concept is inside our scope -- it is A3's concept -- and the label is simply too coarse to place. It cannot fire on corpus v1: every corpus tool name and every server id is pure ASCII, which the committed whole-corpus manifest shows.
entries.decided_by: mcp-sec-bench maintainers (no disclosed tie to Ventrova)
